content.text:
This changes the shape of a few things for the better — the constraints actually sharpen the concept rather than just restricting it. Let me walk through what I'm changing and the assumptions I'm making.

## Revised concept: swap the cardiac trace for the EWS chart

You said the Early Warning Score chart is one of the four things you work from every day. That's a better spine for the site than the ECG trace I proposed — it's not a specialty flourish, it's the actual tool you hand-chart every shift, and it carries a nice double meaning: an EWS exists to catch a system deteriorating before it becomes a serious incident, which is exactly what you do for hospital processes. I'll use a colour-banded trend line (green/amber/red zones, the real EWS visual language) as the scroll spine instead of a generic monitor beep line.

I'll also use the **audit cycle (Plan–Do–Study–Act)** as the structural device for both case studies, rather than a generic "before/after." Each case study scrolls through its own PDSA loop — this is the language clinical informatics hiring managers actually think in, so it'll read as fluency rather than a borrowed template.

## The origin story

I won't use bed 14, initials, or any drug name — agreed, no exceptions. The honest option is to tell it at the level the research poster already operates at: *"a medication very nearly reached the wrong patient, because the scanner lived at the far end of the ward, not beside where the drugs were kept."* No date, no ward-at-the-time, no identifying detail beyond the mechanism — which is also the same systemic finding your research later confirmed independently. I'd want you to read that exact line before it goes anywhere, since "safe enough" is your call to make, not mine.

## Other changes

- **Whiteboard photo is out entirely.** Handover sheets (old and new) shown as blank templates — these actually work well as clean artefacts for the case study.
- **71%→94% reframed as a team outcome**: pharmacy, IT, night staff, and you. Your part stated specifically — forty hours of observation, identifying the three workarounds, getting the scanners relocated to the medication-room door. This is more credible to an informatics-hiring audience than solo-credit framing would have been anyway.
- **Titles corrected everywhere**: "CNM1, Cardiac Step-Down" and "Nursing Informatics Link Nurse (one day a week)." No "Clinical Informatics Lead" on the site at all, including the hero line.
- **Hospital named in plain text, no crest or logo asset** — noted.
- **Handover case study** now credits leading a team of five, and treats ISBAR as something the audience may already know rather than something to explain from scratch — a one-line gloss (Identify, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation), not a tutorial.

## Audience changes the ending

Since this is aimed at people hiring for clinical informatics — hospitals and vendors both — the close of the site needs to work harder than a generic contact block: a plain availability statement (open to clinical informatics roles from 2026), CV download front and center rather than buried, and case studies written in the register those hiring managers actually read in (problem, method, collaborators, your specific contribution, outcome) rather than marketing-case-study voice.

## Assumptions I'm making — flag if wrong

- Exact title string will read as "**CNM1, Cardiac Step-Down · Nursing Informatics Link Nurse**" wherever a title is shown.
- CV download is a plain ATS-friendly PDF, linked prominently, not just in a footer.
- "Looking to do this full time from 2026" gets stated plainly near the contact section, not just implied.
- No other hospital-branded assets (building photos, ward photos) are available or wanted — text mention only, unless you tell me otherwise.
- The genericized near-miss line above is a draft for your approval, not final copy.

I'm saving these constraints to memory now so they carry forward even if this conversation gets summarized later.

Agreed concept for Aoife Brennan's portfolio (not yet built). See [[project-aoife-portfolio-constraints]] for the hard content/privacy rules that override anything below.

**Why:** she wanted an "award-winning," 3D/scroll-driven site that still feels like her work, not a generic agency demo — so the visual language is drawn from her actual clinical tools rather than invented motifs.

**How to apply:**
- Scroll spine = an Early Warning Score (EWS) chart style trend line (colour-banded green/amber/red), not a generic cardiac monitor trace — it's literally one of the four things she charts every shift.
- Each case study structured as a PDSA (Plan-Do-Study-Act) audit cycle, not generic before/after — matches how clinical informatics hiring managers actually think.
- Section order: hero (steady EWS line, name/title) → the why (genericized/anonymized near-miss insight, needs her sign-off) → role (CNM1, Cardiac Step-Down 28 beds, Nursing Informatics Link Nurse 1 day/wk) → case study: ISBAR handover sheet redesign (led team of 5, now on 6 wards, shown as blank templates) → case study: barcode scanning 71%→94% (team effort, her specific contribution called out) → dashboards (falls/pressure ulcer audits, generic numbers only) + conference poster → teaching (preceptor to 14) + MSc Health Informatics in progress → close: explicit availability statement (clinical informatics roles from 2026) + prominent CV PDF download + contact.
- Visual system: dark/charcoal register for reflective sections, warm paper register for process/data sections (night-shift/day-shift duality); alarm red used sparingly for spike moments; monitor teal for data callouts; serif for narrative passages, grotesk mono for numbers/stats, grotesk sans for UI chrome.
- Mobile: WebGL trend line degrades to lighter canvas/SVG driven by scroll position; full `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback (static frames) required everywhere, not just mobile.
- No CMS needed — content is small/static enough to hand-code.
